title: The daily routine
teaches: Run the trading day on three checkpoints: a premarket that reads the futures, the calendar and the news, then narrows the list to a few names with levels, entries, stops and alerts; a midday check on what you hold, your stops and news due later; and a recap after the close that reviews stops, checks tonight's reports and writes tomorrow's plan.

walkthroughs.title: Before the open
steps: Split the day in three: before the open, during the session, after the close.
Start wide. Index futures trade nearly 24 hours, so they show how the market took the overnight news.
Then the calendar. CPI drops at 8:30 a.m. Eastern, and earnings come before the open or after the close.
Then cut your list to the 5 to 10 best setups. Each one gets an entry, a stop and a risk amount.

walkthroughs.title: During the session
steps: Once the bell rings, the action's front-loaded. Volume's heavy early, slows at midday, and picks up into the close.
Midday is a check, not a hunt. Look at what you own and where your stops sit.
Then check what's due later, like a 2:00 p.m. Fed statement.
The rules you wrote stay the rules. Changes wait until the market's closed.

walkthroughs.title: After the close
steps: After the bell, start with what you own. Check each stop. A new higher low is your chance to raise it.
Check who reports tonight or before tomorrow's open. News after the close can gap a stock right past your stop.
Then log today's ideas and write tomorrow's list and levels.
Do that work while the market's closed. The best-planned days tend to give the best results.

questions.q: It's 8:30 a.m. ET, an hour before the 9:30 open. S&P 500 futures are trading lower. What's that telling you?
choices: How the market's taking overnight news
Exactly where stocks will open
Which stocks will lead today
Nothing, futures don't matter for stocks
questions.answer: How the market's taking overnight news
questions.why: It's the market's read on the overnight news. S&P 500 futures trade nearly 24 hours, so they react while stocks sit closed. That's why I check them first thing. SPY's premarket quotes move with them, and a big gap drags the largest index names along too. But it's a hint, not a promise. The opening price gets set by buyers and sellers right at 9:30, and premarket prices don't always stick. Read the futures for the mood, then let the open confirm it.
questions.lesson_line: Futures are the market's overnight vote. Read the mood, then let the open confirm it.

wrong.Exactly where stocks will open: Nobody knows that before 9:30. The open gets set by supply and demand at the bell, and premarket prices don't always hold.
wrong.Which stocks will lead today: Futures track the whole index, all 500 names at once. They can't tell you which ones lead. Your list and relative strength do that.
wrong.Nothing, futures don't matter for stocks: They matter. SPY moves with them before the open, and a big gap moves the biggest names in the index too.

questions.simple: They show how the market is taking the overnight news, since the futures trade nearly around the clock.

questions.q: The middle of the trading day is when the market is busiest and moves the most.
questions.why: False. Midday's the quiet part. Volume comes in heavy at the open, often slows into lunch, and picks back up into the close. The first and last hours are where the action and the big swings are. So I treat midday as a check-in, not a hunt. Look at what you own and what's on the calendar. One catch: big news like a Fed rate announcement can flip that pattern on a given day.
questions.lesson_line: Busy open, quiet lunch, busy close. Do your midday check in the quiet part.
questions.simple: False. The open and the close are the busy times, and the middle of the day is the quiet stretch.

questions.q: You're building tomorrow's watchlist. What earns a stock a spot on it?
choices: It meets your setup criteria
It was today's biggest gainer
A chat room is buzzing about it
questions.why: It meets your setup criteria. A watchlist holds the names that fit your rules, so you can watch them for an entry signal.
questions.lesson_line: The list is for names that fit your setups, not names that are loud.

wrong.It was today's biggest gainer: A big day can be part of a setup, but on its own it's just a move. The list holds names that meet your criteria.
wrong.A chat room is buzzing about it: Buzz isn't a criterion. Investopedia warns that many chat-room posters have ulterior motives. Check the name against your own rules.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The economic ___ lists the scheduled reports and events that can move the whole market.
questions.why: Calendar. The economic calendar lists the scheduled dates of big reports and events that can move a stock or the whole market. It covers reports such as jobless claims and interest rate announcements. BLS, for one, posts its release dates and times in Eastern Time.
questions.lesson_line: Check the economic calendar every premarket. A scheduled report can move the whole market.
questions.simple: Calendar, because the economic calendar is the list of dates when big reports and events come out.

questions.q: Your focus list has four names, each with a trigger level marked. How do you catch the moment one trades through?
choices: Set price alerts at each trigger
Keep flipping through the charts
Buy all four now so none get away
Check them once, right at the open
questions.answer: Set price alerts at each trigger
questions.why: Set alerts. Put a price alert right at each trigger, and the stock tells you when it gets there. Then you look. Flip through charts instead and you'll be on the wrong one when the right one moves. An alert only says when to look, though. You still check the entry, the stop and the size before you buy.
questions.lesson_line: Let alerts do the watching. You show up when a level trades.

wrong.Keep flipping through the charts: You'll catch some and miss others. While you're on one chart, another trades through its level.
wrong.Buy all four now so none get away: That's buying before any of them trigger. The plan was to buy the break, not to hope for one.
wrong.Check them once, right at the open: A level can trade any time in the session. One look at the open misses everything after it.

questions.simple: Set alerts at your triggers, so the market tells you when to look instead of you watching every chart.

deeper.example: SMB trader Steve Spencer loads alerts at key prices into his platform before the open. Gatis Roze, a veteran full-time trader, spends his early morning reviewing charts and adjusting alerts. Same idea both ways: the alert watches, you decide.

questions.q: During the session, you trade the rules you wrote before the open and save any changes for after the close.
questions.why: True. While the market's open you execute. You don't rewrite. In the moment, a fast drop or a big green candle makes every rule feel wrong. That's exactly when changes are worst, because they come from impulse, not thinking. So the entry and stop rules stay put. After the close, with the market shut, you look calmly and fix what needs fixing. Reading the market as it moves is fine. Rewriting your rules mid-session isn't.
questions.lesson_line: During the session you execute. Rule changes wait for the close.
questions.simple: True. During the session you follow your rules, and any change waits until the market is closed and you can think.

questions.q: Your scan turns up a chart that looks perfect. Before you plan the buy, what else does your premarket check?
choices: The market's trend and its sector
Nothing, a great chart is enough
Analysts' price targets for it
How much buzz it has on social media
questions.answer: The market's trend and its sector
questions.why: The market and the sector. A stock almost never runs on its own while its group goes nowhere. And even a short-term trade works better going the same way as the bigger trend. So before I plan any buy, I check the market's trend and the stock's group. The app's market reading gives you the first part at a glance. If both line up, that perfect chart has the wind at its back. If the market's rolling over, even great charts can drop fast. The chart still matters. It's just not the whole check.
questions.lesson_line: Market first, then the group, then the stock.

wrong.Nothing, a great chart is enough: Charts don't trade in a vacuum. Fight the bigger trend and even a great setup gets dragged down.
wrong.Analysts' price targets for it: A target is someone's guess at a price. It tells you nothing about whether the market's helping or hurting today.
wrong.How much buzz it has on social media: Buzz isn't a reason to buy. Boards and chat rooms are full of people with their own motives.

questions.simple: Check the market's trend and the stock's group. Trades work better with the trend, and leaders tend to sit in strong groups.

deeper.example: O'Neil's CAN SLIM checks the market's direction every day from the major averages. Gatis Roze, a veteran full-time trader, says a stock rising all by itself is so rare it isn't worth considering. He means apart from its sector and its group.

questions.story: CPI morning. The report's due at 8:30 a.m. ET. By 8:00 your plan is set: three names, each with a trigger, a stop and a size.
questions.q: What's the play this morning?
choices: Read the futures, then run the plan
Sit out the day until CPI is priced in
Scrap the plan and start over
Buy all three before it comes out
questions.answer: Read the futures, then run the plan
questions.why: Read the futures, then run the plan. We don't have a news-day rule. Fed and CPI days get traded like any other day. CPI lands at 8:30, an hour before stocks open at 9:30. So the futures take the hit first, and you get to watch how the market takes the number. Then the open comes, your triggers trade or they don't, and your stops do their job. What you don't do is guess the number. I'd rather react to what the market does with it.
questions.lesson_line: Know when the report hits. Read the reaction, then run the plan.

wrong.Scrap the plan and start over: A report isn't a reason to tear up a plan you built with a clear head. Let the futures react, then run it.
wrong.Buy all three before it comes out: That's a bet on a number nobody's seen, in thin premarket trading. And we don't make new buys outside regular hours anyway.
wrong.Sit out the day until CPI is priced in: We don't have a news-day rule. CPI days get traded like any other day, and your stops are already in place.

questions.simple: Watch how the futures take the report, then run your plan, because we trade CPI days like any other day.

reasons: a release time (CPI 8:30 a.m. ET) that changes by date
rests on the owner's rulebook (C32, E58)

questions.q: S&P 500 futures were at 6,000 at 4:00 p.m. yesterday. At 8:45 a.m. today they're at 5,940. How far down is that?
questions.why: Down 1%. Take the drop first: 6,000 minus 5,940 is 60 points. Then divide by where you started: 60 over 6,000 is 1%. Always measure from yesterday's 4:00 level, not from today's number. Sixty points sounds scary and tells you nothing on its own. One percent you can compare to any other morning. A 1% red premarket hints at a soft open. Premarket prices don't always hold though, so I wait for the open before I worry.
questions.lesson_line: Read futures in percent, not points. Sixty points means little until you size it against the level.
questions.simple: Down 1%, because the 60 point drop is one percent of the 6,000 level where the futures started.

wrong.60%: That's the 60 points read as a percent. Points aren't percent until you divide by 6,000.
wrong.10%: A decimal slip. 60 over 6,000 is one hundredth, so 1%, not ten times that.
wrong.99%: That's 5,940 as a share of 6,000. You skipped taking it away from the whole.

questions.q: Premarket. You've marked yesterday's open, high, low and close on a name you might buy today. Which level is your stop built from?
choices: Yesterday's low
Yesterday's high
Yesterday's close
Yesterday's open
questions.why: Yesterday's low. Our stop goes a few cents under the low of the day or the prior day's low. Before the open, today's low doesn't exist yet. So yesterday's low is the one you can mark, and size from, right now. A low is where the chart says you're wrong. Trade back under the level buyers defended yesterday and the setup failed, so you want out. A few cents under it, not right on it, so a tick of noise doesn't take you out.
questions.lesson_line: Mark yesterday's high and low on every name. The stop goes a few cents under a low.

wrong.Yesterday's high: Worth marking, it can be a trigger. But a long's stop sits under a low, where the chart says you're wrong.
wrong.Yesterday's close: Good context, but nobody defended the close. The stop goes a few cents under a low.
wrong.Yesterday's open: Worth marking, but it's not where buyers stepped in. Our stop sits a few cents under a low.

questions.simple: Yesterday's low, because our stop sits just under a low and today's low doesn't exist yet before the open.

reasons: key rests on one house fact (h1)
rests on the owner's rulebook (sizing_rule.md section 2 and F62)

questions.story: Sunday night your scans leave you 45 names. Monday you get 20 minutes of prep before work.
questions.q: What do you do with that list tonight?
choices: Narrow it to the few best setups
Watch all 45 and react to movers
Buy a little of each to be safe
Add more names so you miss nothing
questions.answer: Narrow it to the few best setups
questions.why: Cut it down tonight. We keep a focus list of the 5 to 10 best setups each day, and the rest get ignored. Twenty minutes in the morning won't cover 45 charts, that's under half a minute a chart. So the ranking happens tonight, while the market's closed and you can think. Give each name that makes it a trigger, a stop, a size and an alert. Then Monday's 20 minutes go to checking that short list against the futures and the news. A few names watched closely beat 45 watched badly.
questions.lesson_line: Narrow your list. The best names get your attention, the rest wait.

wrong.Watch all 45 and react to movers: You can't follow 45 names closely. Reacting to whatever moves turns into chasing.
wrong.Buy a little of each to be safe: That's a pile of trades with no trigger, stop or size behind any of them. Small and sloppy isn't safe.
wrong.Add more names so you miss nothing: More names means less attention on each. You miss the good one because you're busy with the rest.

questions.simple: Narrow it to the few best setups tonight, because 20 minutes can't cover 45 charts and a short list gets real attention.

deeper.example: Sunday night, 45 names pass your scan. Rank them by how clean each setup is. Keep the best 5 to 10 and give each one levels, an entry, a stop, a size and an alert. Monday's 20 minutes then go to checking that short list against the futures and the news, not to finding it. Trading coach Brett Steenbarger saw the same in pro traders. Ranking ideas during prep is what lets them act fast when one sets up.

questions.story: Your plan: buy over $50, stop at $48, so $2 of risk a share. Overnight news hits, and the stock gaps up. At 9:45 a.m. it trades at $53.50.
questions.q: If you bought here at $53.50, what would each share risk?
choices: $5.50, up from the planned $2
Still $2, the stop didn't move
$3.50, how far it gapped past $50
Less, the move is in my favor
questions.why: $5.50 a share, not $2. Risk per share is entry minus stop: $53.50 minus $48 is $5.50. The stop didn't move, but your entry did. Each share now risks almost three times what you planned. And we wouldn't take this one anyway. We never buy more than 4% above the buy point, and $3.50 over a $50 trigger is way past that. Chase it at the old size and the trade risks far more than you meant to. If you missed it, you missed it. Let it set up again.
questions.lesson_line: A gap rewrites the plan's math. Never buy on the old numbers.

wrong.Still $2, the stop didn't move: The stop stayed, but you paid more. It's $53.50 minus $48 now, not $50 minus $48.
wrong.$3.50, how far it gapped past $50: That's how far it ran past your trigger, not how far down your stop is.
wrong.Less, the move is in my favor: Paying more for the same stop means more risk a share, not less.

questions.simple: $5.50, because risk per share is entry minus stop, and $53.50 minus $48 is $5.50.

deeper.trap: The trap is the stop that didn't move. It feels like the plan still holds. But risk per share is entry minus stop, so at $53.50 each share risks $5.50, not $2. Buy the share count you planned for $2 of risk a share, and the trade risks far more than you meant.

reasons: story moved into the session in wave9 (E58)

questions.q: 12:30 p.m. The market's gone quiet and you've got a few minutes. What do you look at first?
choices: Positions, stops and news due later
A fresh scan for new names to buy
Lower stops to give trades more room
Close it all out while it's quiet
questions.answer: Positions, stops and news due later
questions.why: What you own. Check your positions, where each stop sits, and what's scheduled later, like a 2:00 Fed statement. Protecting what you already have comes before hunting for more. A new buy can't help you if an old one is quietly breaking down. So look for new support on your holdings and a chance to raise a stop. Then the calendar, because big news mid-session can flip a quiet afternoon fast. New buys can come after. They just don't come first.
questions.lesson_line: Midday is a check, not a hunt.

wrong.A fresh scan for new names to buy: New buys can wait. Protect what you own first.
wrong.Lower stops to give trades more room: A long's stop only moves up, never down. Lowering it adds risk you never planned.
wrong.Close it all out while it's quiet: Quiet at lunch is normal, and volume picks back up into the close. A swing trade runs on its plan and its stop, not the clock.

questions.simple: Check what you own, your stops and the news due later, because protecting your trades comes before hunting for new ones.

deeper.example: Gatis Roze, a veteran full-time trader, does the same at midday. He shifts his focus to what he owns, because protection takes precedence over searching out fresh new purchases.

questions.story: At 2:00 p.m. the market whips both ways, and your stock swings through your stop and back. Later you learn the Fed's statement came out at 2:00.
questions.q: What in your premarket would've had you ready for that?
choices: Checking the day's economic calendar
Reading the overnight index futures
Marking levels on each of your names
Scanning company news on your names
questions.why: The economic calendar. It lists the scheduled reports and events that can move the whole market, Fed rate announcements included. The Fed's Oct. 28, 2026 statement came out at 2:00 p.m. ET, right in the middle of the session. One look at the calendar that morning and the 2:00 whipsaw isn't a surprise. It tells you when to expect a jolt, not which way it goes. We don't sit out Fed days, they trade like any other day. You just know it's coming.
questions.lesson_line: Levels tell you where. The calendar tells you when.

wrong.Reading the overnight index futures: Futures show the overnight mood. They don't tell you what's scheduled at 2:00.
wrong.Marking levels on each of your names: Levels tell you where to act, not when the market's about to jolt.
wrong.Scanning company news on your names: Company news matters, but a Fed statement hits the whole market on a schedule. That's on the economic calendar.

questions.simple: Checking the economic calendar, because it lists scheduled events like a Fed statement that can jolt the whole market.

questions.story: After the close you run your recap. One holding just made a new higher low, well above your stop.
questions.q: What does the recap do with that stop?
choices: Consider raising it under that low
Consider lowering it for more room
Cancel it, since the trade is working
Raise it to today's closing price
questions.answer: Consider raising it under that low
questions.why: Consider raising it under that low. Each day, review open positions for new support levels and chances to adjust your stops. Support is usually a previous low, so a new higher low is the natural place to look. Our rule: the stop only moves up, never down or wider. Raising it is a judgment, not a must.
questions.lesson_line: Stops move one way: in the direction of the trade.

wrong.Cancel it, since the trade is working: Working trades can turn. Without a stop, a winner can become a loser.
wrong.Consider lowering it for more room: Our stop only moves up, never down or wider. Widening a stop on a winner adds risk for no reason.
wrong.Raise it to today's closing price: Support is usually a previous low, not a close. The new higher low is the level the trade should hold, so a raised stop goes under it.

questions.simple: Consider raising it to just under the new low, because a stop only moves up, in the direction of the trade.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4); may meet his trail rule E52 (owner flag)
key and one distractor reworded for balance

questions.story: You work 9 to 5 and can't watch the market. You hold two swing trades, each with a planned stop.
questions.q: Where do those stops live while you're at work?
choices: As stop orders at your broker
In your head, a lunch check
Nowhere until you get home
As alerts on your phone
questions.answer: As stop orders at your broker
questions.why: Stop orders at your broker. Every position we hold has a real stop order sitting with the broker, not a number in your head. While you're in a meeting, a mental stop does nothing, and the stock can keep falling until you look. A resting order sells on its own. It's not a guarantee, though. If the stock gaps past your stop, the fill can land lower and cost more than you planned. Still a lot better than no stop at all.
questions.lesson_line: If you can't watch, your stops have to be real orders, not intentions.

wrong.In your head, a lunch check: Between checks, nothing sells. A stop in your head only works when you're watching.
wrong.Nowhere until you get home: Then a bad day has no floor until 5. That's a loss you never planned.
wrong.As alerts on your phone: An alert tells you the price traded. If you can't act on it at work, nothing sells.

questions.simple: Real stop orders at your broker, because an order sells on its own while you're at work and can't watch.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking a stop order caps the loss exactly. It doesn't. If the stock gaps past your stop, the loss can be bigger than you planned, even with proper sizing. Size the trade knowing a gap can skip it.
deeper.counter: Some traders who watch all session, like Gatis Roze, use mental stops instead of orders with the broker. That works when you're at the screen. We still keep a real order in, and if you can't watch, you need it.

questions.story: You skipped Monday's recap and Tuesday's prep. At 4:05 p.m. Tuesday, a stock you hold reports. It falls 11% after hours.
questions.q: What would have saved you from that 11% drop?
choices: Checking earnings dates for holdings
Reading the futures each morning
A tighter stop on that holding
The midday check on market volume
questions.why: Knowing the earnings date. Most companies report before the open or after the close. A weak report after the bell can drop a stock fast after hours. That's why the recap checks who reports tonight and tomorrow morning. We only hold through a report if the trade's up 5R, five times what you risked. Short of that, you sell before the close. Spot the date Monday and you'd have had all of Tuesday's session to decide. A tighter stop wouldn't have helped. The report hits after the bell, and the stock opens wherever it opens.
questions.lesson_line: Every day, check who reports tonight and tomorrow morning. Decide before the close, not after the gap.

wrong.Reading the futures each morning: Futures show the market's mood. They don't tell you when your company reports.
wrong.A tighter stop on that holding: A stop can't stop a report. The stock gaps right past it, and your fill comes at the next open, far below.
wrong.The midday check on market volume: Volume says nothing about a report date. The earnings calendar does.

questions.simple: Checking earnings dates on what you hold, because knowing the date lets you decide before the close, not after the gap.

deeper.trap: A tighter stop feels like protection here. It isn't. The report lands at 4:05 p.m., after the close, so the stock can open far below the stop the next morning. A gap past your stop can cost more than you planned. What works is knowing the date and applying our rule before the close.

questions.q: You only get 20 minutes before work, so a premarket routine isn't worth having.
questions.why: False. Twenty minutes is plenty if the heavy lifting's already done. Build the routine around the day you really have. Do the list, the levels and the stops the night before. Then the morning is a quick check: the futures, the calendar, news on your names, alerts set. A short routine you run every day beats a long one you skip. Skip it entirely and you're trading the open on impulse.
questions.lesson_line: Build the routine around the day you really have.
questions.simple: False. A short routine built around your real day still works, as long as the planning is done the night before.

deeper.example: Gatis Roze says to design your routines around the time limits of your existing day. SMB's Steve Spencer runs a set morning list that packs a lot of information into a short window.

questions.story: For three weeks the S&P 500 has made lower highs and lower lows. Most names on your list broke support. One chart still looks perfect.
questions.q: How do you treat that one name?
choices: Track it, the market's against it
Full size, it held when others broke
Buy the broken names, they're cheap
Short it, the market is falling
questions.answer: Track it, the market's against it
questions.why: Track it, don't force it. Three weeks of lower highs and lower lows is a downtrend, and you don't fight that. Trades work better with the bigger trend. When the market turns hard, even strong stocks can drop fast. But a name that holds up while most of your list breaks is showing relative strength. That's the one you want on your radar. Check our market filter in the app first. In Orange we only take A+ setups, our cleanest. In Red we're mostly cash. So it stays on watch, and you only buy if it sets up clean. If the market turns, a name like this can be one of the first to lead.
questions.lesson_line: In a falling market, the name that holds up goes on your radar. Let it prove itself first.

wrong.Full size, it held when others broke: Holding up earns it a spot on your radar, not full size. Even strong stocks can drop fast once the market turns.
wrong.Buy the broken names, they're cheap: Broken support isn't a discount. The old low turns into overhead, and sellers show up on the way back up.
wrong.Short it, the market is falling: We short the weakest stocks in the weakest groups. A chart that still looks perfect is the opposite.

questions.simple: Track it but don't force it, because even strong stocks can drop fast while the market is falling.

deeper.trap: The trap is the one chart that holds up while everything around it breaks. It feels like strength, and sometimes it is. But even strong stocks can drop fast when the market turns. Treat it as a name to watch closely, not a reason to ignore the market.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65, C31)

questions.q: Even after decades of trading, it pays to run your daily routine from a written checklist.
questions.why: True. Gatis Roze has traded his own account full time since 1989, and he still works from written checklists. He keeps them in sight, because out of sight is out of mind. The list tells him what's next and when the job is done. On a busy morning, memory skips steps. The one you skip is the earnings date or the stop you meant to raise. A written list doesn't skip. I'd keep yours somewhere you see it every morning.
questions.lesson_line: Out of sight is out of mind. Write the routine down and keep it where you can see it.
questions.simple: True. Veterans still use written checklists kept in plain sight, because memory skips steps on a busy morning.

questions.story: Down day. You took two small losses, both by the plan, and still hold three names. It's 4:10 p.m., and you want to shut the laptop and forget it.
questions.q: What do you still do tonight?
choices: Stops, reports due, tomorrow's list
Nothing, a red day earns you a break
A bigger list to win it back
Looser stops, so they don't hit
questions.why: The full recap, red day or not. Check the stop on each of the three names you still hold. Check who reports tonight or tomorrow morning. Write tomorrow's list while the market's closed. And journal both losses today, while they're fresh. Two small losses taken by the plan mean the plan worked. That's the cost of trading, not a reason to quit early. What you don't do is build a bigger list to win it back. That's revenge trading, and it backfires.
questions.lesson_line: Red day or green day, the recap runs. It's how tomorrow starts.

wrong.A bigger list to win it back: That's revenge trading. Trading more to make back a loss is how a small red day turns into a big one.
wrong.Looser stops, so they don't hit: Our stop only moves up, never down or wider. Loosen it and the next loss is just bigger.
wrong.Nothing, a red day earns you a break: The three names you still hold don't care how your day felt. Their stops and tomorrow's plan still need you.

questions.simple: Check your stops, see who reports, and write tomorrow's list, because the recap sets up tomorrow however today felt.

deeper.trap: The trap is the urge after a red day. Shutting the laptop skips the stops on the three names you still hold. A bigger list to win it back is revenge trading. Widening stops breaks our rule: the stop only moves up. Two small losses taken by the plan mean the plan worked. The recap keeps it working.

questions.story: You work days. You get 20 minutes before work and about an hour after 5 p.m.
questions.q: Where does the real planning happen?
choices: Evenings: list, levels, stops, size
Mornings: scan everything from scratch
Lunch break: scan and buy midday
Skip prep and react to the open
questions.why: Evenings. The hour after 5 is your longest window, and the market's closed, so you can think. That's when the list, the levels, the stops and the size get built. Every planned buy has its entry, stop and size written down before the open. Then the 20 minutes in the morning are just a check: the futures, the calendar, news on your names. Try to build the plan in 20 minutes and you'll rush it. Then you're reacting to the open, one of the wildest hours of the day.
questions.lesson_line: Build the plan at night. Use the morning to check it, not to write it.

wrong.Mornings: scan everything from scratch: There's no time for that. Twenty minutes is for checking the plan, not building it.
wrong.Lunch break: scan and buy midday: Midday is for checking what you hold. The plan gets built while the market's closed.
wrong.Skip prep and react to the open: Then you decide on impulse, with no entry, stop or size written down before the open.

questions.simple: Evenings, because that's your longest window and the market is closed, so the short morning only checks the plan.

deeper.trap: The trap is the morning scan. Twenty minutes feels like prep time, but it can't build a list, levels and stops from scratch. Rushed, you end up reacting to the open, and the opening hour is one of the most volatile of the day. Build the list at night, and use the morning only to check it.

questions.story: After the close you run your recap. One holding is a fast mover, well above your stop and riding its rising averages.
questions.q: Tonight's recap. What are you checking on it?
choices: Check for a close below the 9 EMA
Look for a close below the 20 EMA
Cancel the stop, it's working
Raise the stop to today's close
questions.answer: Check for a close below the 9 EMA
questions.why: Whether it closed under the 9 EMA. On a fast mover, the 9 EMA is our trail. On a steadier name it's the 20 EMA. We sell what's left on a close below it, so the recap after the close is exactly when you check. A dip under the 9 during the day doesn't count. The close decides. Trail a fast mover on the 20 and you hand back more of the run. And the stop itself only ever moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Stops only move up. On a fast mover, the 9 EMA is the trail, checked at the close.
questions.simple: Check for a close below the 9 EMA, because that's our trail for a fast mover.

wrong.Cancel the stop, it's working: The stop's your exit. Cancel it and a working trade has no exit if it turns.
wrong.Raise the stop to today's close: Our trail is the rising average, not the close. On a fast mover, that's the 9 EMA.
wrong.Look for a close below the 20 EMA: That's the trail for steadier names. On a fast mover, the 20 sits further back and gives away more of the move.

reasons: re-keyed in wave9 to the owner's rulebook (E52, A4)

conflicts: Premarket start time: Investopedia (s13) says premarket trading runs from 4 a.m. ET; FINRA (s6) says it is 'typically defined as taking place from 7 - 9:30 a.m. ET'; brokers differ. The unit never keys a premarket start time (F1.05 owns session hours).

No single order for the premarket: Steenbarger (s40) starts with overseas markets, the day's economic reports, yesterday's indicators and overnight Globex; Roze (s35, s32) starts with the news, the Nasdaq premarket pages and overseas markets, then runs top-down (market trends, then sectors, then stocks); Spencer (s41) runs platforms, his game plan, alerts, a scanner and his journal. Investopedia's 10 Steps (s17) looks at the stock first and then steps back to the market, the reverse of Roze's top-down. So no question keys a fixed order of steps. The unit keys only what they share: plan when the market is closed (q06, q22), know the calendar (q04, q08, q14), narrow the list (q11), set levels, stops and alerts (q05, q10), and read the market as well as the stock (q07, q19). The row's 'P: order the routine' is taught that way.

Steenbarger (t2) modifies his game plan as the morning reports come out, while Investopedia (it1) and Fidelity (fp1) say the plan's rules should not change while you are trading. Not a contradiction: Steenbarger adjusts his read of the market; the entry and stop rules stay. q06 keys the rules; q08 keys adjusting the plan to the report.

Trading the open: Investopedia's beginner day-trading guide (s16) suggests novices watch the first 15-20 minutes, and Roze (s35) is 'seldom active' in the first hour, while Investopedia's timing piece (s14) says many professionals focus on the opening hour. The unit never keys whether to trade the open.

Mental vs hard stops: Roze (rf2) uses 'soft' (mental) stops because he watches all session. q16 keys only the case of a member who cannot watch (a resting stop order), with Schwab (sb5) and the gap caveat (ips2); it does not say mental stops are wrong for someone at the screen.

Roze's StockCharts articles date from 2012-2013. They are cited only for process advice that does not expire (write routines down, fit them to your day, plan when the market is closed, check the group). His lunchtime 'manipulation' view and the Trader's Almanac last-half-hour statistic in the same series are not used.

Investopedia's economic-calendar page (s19) suggests a trader who 'guesses correctly' can open a position right before an announcement. That is a gamble on an unseen number, and the unit teaches the opposite (q08 wrong choice 'Buy all three before it comes out'); only the page's definition of the calendar (ie1) is cited.

Futures hours: Investopedia's E-mini page gives Sunday-Friday 6 p.m. to 5 p.m. ET with a 5-6 p.m. halt, but CME's own contract-spec table loads by script and could not be read as page text. The unit says only 'nearly 24 hours' (CME's own product page, fc1) and never keys exact futures hours.

Unit plan row 'covers': course M6 'premarket routine' and dossier M12 are docs/curriculum, which the contract forbids as a source; not used. The Journal day-notes shape (prep, mid-day, recap) matches the unit's three checkpoints, but no house page states a routine in the owner's words, so the only house question (q10) rests on the owner's default stop (sizing_rule.md section 2), which F9.02 also asks directly; q10 asks it from the premarket angle (before the open only yesterday's low exists).

Overlap with F8.07 (the daily MENTAL routine, same Steenbarger morning posts): F8.07 owns the warm-up of the trader, breaks and the emotional cool-down; this unit owns the market and process side (futures, calendar, list, levels, alerts, midday check, the mechanical recap). Facts shared with F8.07 (Spencer's morning list, Steenbarger's game plan) are asked here from a different angle. Overlap with F7.07 (release times), F5.04 (earnings timing) and F1.05 / F10.04 (extended hours): those facts appear here only inside routine decisions, never asked as the same recall question.

Source check (checker, 2026-11-09): Investopedia's pre-market page (s13) now refuses every automated client (HTTP 402/403 to curl, the quote checker and WebFetch; the Wayback Machine's 2026 capture is also a 402). Its four quotes (ip1, ip2, ip3, ip5) were confirmed word for word on the Wayback Machine capture of 2025-08-21 (page 'Updated August 15, 2025', James Chen). The writer's 'updated 2026-09-17' could not be confirmed and was dropped from the title. They are evergreen market-structure facts; q01 and q09 also rest on CME's own page (fc1, fc5).

w1.notes: rp1 (Roze), fc1 (CME), fb1+fb2 (BLS: Oct CPI Tue Nov 10 2026, 08:30 AM, all times ET), fe1 (FINRA), iw3, t4 (Spencer: entries/stops/targets/risk amount) all confirmed on the live pages, read in context. Changed: 'companies report before the open or after the close' to 'usually report', because FINRA's quote says 'usually'.
